q: An atom has 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 11 electrons. What is its mass number?
why: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23.

q: What was the main conclusion of the alpha particle scattering experiment?
c: The mass of an atom is concentrated in a small, positive nucleus
why: Most alpha particles passed straight through, but a few were deflected strongly, showing a tiny dense positive nucleus.

q: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
c: They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell
why: Reactions depend on outer-shell electrons, which group members share.

q: How does reactivity change going down group 1?
why: The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

q: Which is a typical property of transition metals compared with group 1 metals?
c: They react vigorously with cold water
why: Transition metals have higher melting points and densities, and form coloured compounds and ions with different charges.

q: Which use of transition metals depends on them speeding up reactions?
c: Catalysts, such as iron in the Haber process
why: Many transition metals and their compounds are catalysts.

q: What forms when magnesium reacts with oxygen?
c: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions in an ionic compound
why: Magnesium transfers two electrons to oxygen, forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.

q: What holds atoms together in a covalent bond?
why: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms.

q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
c: They have delocalised electrons that move through the structure
why: Delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal.

q: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?
c: Different-sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide easily
why: Atoms of a different size disrupt the regular layers, making it harder for them to slide.

q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
c: Each carbon has one delocalised electron
Its layers are held by covalent bonds
why: Each carbon forms three bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom.

q: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
c: Many strong covalent bonds in a giant structure
why: Melting diamond means breaking many strong covalent bonds.

q: Why can nanoparticles be more effective catalysts than larger particles of the same material?
c: They have a much higher surface area to volume ratio
why: More of the atoms are at the surface, where reactions happen.

q: What is the size range of nanoparticles?
why: Nanoparticles are 1–100 nm across (a few hundred atoms).

q: What is the relative formula mass (Mr) of CO₂? (C = 12, O = 16)
Which equation is balanced?
why: Both sides have 4 H and 2 O atoms.

q: How many moles are in 36 g of water? (Mr of H₂O = 18)
why: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 36 ÷ 18 = 2.

q: What is the limiting reactant?
c: The reactant that is completely used up and limits the product
why: Once the limiting reactant runs out, no more product can form.

q: A reaction could make 50 g of product but makes 40 g. What is the percentage yield?
Why is a high atom economy important?
c: Fewer atoms end up in waste products, so it is more sustainable
It means no catalyst is needed
why: A high atom economy means more of the reactants become the useful product.

q: 25 g of salt is dissolved to make 0.5 dm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
why: Concentration = mass ÷ volume = 25 ÷ 0.5 = 50 g/dm³.

q: How many cm³ are in 1 dm³?
why: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.

q: What volume does one mole of any gas occupy at room temperature and pressure?
why: One mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at RTP.

q: What volume does 0.5 mol of oxygen occupy at room temperature and pressure?
Which metal can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon?
why: Only metals less reactive than carbon, like iron, can be reduced by carbon.

q: Iron is added to copper sulfate solution. What happens?
c: Iron displaces copper, forming iron sulfate
why: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it from its compound.

q: What salt forms when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
why: Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

q: What are the products when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
c: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
why: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.

q: In the electrolysis of molten lead bromide, what forms at the cathode?
why: Positive lead ions are attracted to the negative cathode and gain electrons.

q: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved for electrolysis?
c: So the ions are free to move
why: Ions are fixed in a solid lattice; they must be able to move to the electrodes.

q: Which is an endothermic process?
why: Thermal decomposition takes in energy; the others release it.

q: What does a reaction profile show for an exothermic reaction?
c: Products higher in energy than reactants
Products lower in energy than reactants
Reactants and products at the same energy
why: Energy is released to the surroundings, so the products end lower.

q: What is the only waste product of a hydrogen fuel cell?
why: Hydrogen and oxygen react to give water.

q: Why does a simple chemical cell eventually stop working?
c: One of the reactants is used up
why: A cell stops once a reactant runs out; non-rechargeable cells cannot be reversed.

q: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction?
c: Particles move faster, collide more often and more collisions have enough energy
why: Faster particles collide more often and more of the collisions reach the activation energy.

q: Why does powdered calcium carbonate react faster than lumps of the same mass?
c: It has a larger surface area
why: A greater surface area means more frequent collisions.

q: In a reversible reaction at equilibrium, the pressure is increased. Which way does the equilibrium shift?
c: Towards the side with more gas molecules
Towards the side with fewer gas molecules
why: The system counteracts the increase by favouring the side with fewer gas molecules.

q: What symbol shows a reversible reaction?
why: The double half-arrow shows a reaction that can go both ways.

q: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
why: Alkanes are saturated: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, e.g. methane CH₄.

q: Why is cracking useful?
c: It turns long hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful ones and alkenes
It separates crude oil into fractions
why: Cracking meets demand for short-chain fuels and makes alkenes for polymers.

q: What is the test for an alkene?
c: Bromine water turns from orange to colourless
why: Alkenes add bromine across the double bond, decolourising bromine water.

q: Which functional group do all alcohols contain?
why: Alcohols contain the –OH group; carboxylic acids contain –COOH.

q: What forms when many ethene molecules join together?
why: Addition polymerisation joins ethene monomers into poly(ethene).

q: What small molecule is usually released in condensation polymerisation?
why: Each link formed in condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule, usually water.

q: How can you tell a substance is pure?
c: It melts and boils at a fixed temperature
why: Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points.

q: A spot moves 3 cm and the solvent front moves 6 cm. What is the Rf value?
why: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5.

q: What is the test for carbon dioxide?
c: It burns with a squeaky pop
why: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky (cloudy).

q: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
why: Oxygen relights a glowing splint.

q: Which metal ion gives a lilac flame?
why: Potassium gives lilac; sodium yellow; lithium crimson; calcium orange-red.

q: Sodium hydroxide is added to a solution and a blue precipitate forms. Which ion is present?
why: Copper(II) hydroxide is a blue precipitate.

q: What are roughly the proportions of nitrogen and oxygen in the air today?
c: About four-fifths nitrogen and one-fifth oxygen
why: The atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

q: How did oxygen first build up in Earth's atmosphere?
why: Algae and later plants released oxygen through photosynthesis.

q: Which human activity releases methane?
why: Livestock digestion and rice paddies release methane, a greenhouse gas.

q: How do greenhouse gases warm the Earth?
c: They absorb ultraviolet from the Sun
They absorb infrared radiated from the Earth's surface and re-emit it
They reflect sunlight back to Earth
why: They absorb long-wave infrared from the surface, keeping energy in the atmosphere.

q: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous?
c: It is toxic: it stops blood carrying oxygen
It is a greenhouse gas only
why: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, reducing the oxygen the blood can carry.

q: Which pollutant causes acid rain?
why: Sulfur dioxide (and nitrogen oxides) dissolve in rain to make it acidic.

q: What makes water potable?
c: It is safe to drink, with low levels of salts and microbes
It contains no minerals at all
why: Potable water is safe to drink; it is not chemically pure.

q: Which step is used to sterilise drinking water?
why: Sterilising agents kill microbes after filtration.

q: What does a life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluate?
c: Only the cost of a product
The environmental impact of a product at every stage, from raw materials to disposal
why: An LCA looks at extraction, manufacture, use and disposal.

q: Why is recycling metals usually better than extracting new metal?
c: It uses less energy and conserves finite ores
why: Recycling saves energy and limited resources and reduces mining waste.

q: What two substances does iron need to rust?
why: Rusting needs both air (oxygen) and water.

q: Why is galvanising (coating with zinc) good protection for iron?
c: Zinc is less reactive than iron
Zinc reacts in preference to iron, even if scratched
why: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron (sacrificial protection).

q: What are the raw materials for the Haber process?
why: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Nitrogen comes from air, hydrogen from natural gas.

q: Which conditions are used in the Haber process?
c: About 450 °C, 200 atm and an iron catalyst
About 450 °C, 1 atm and a platinum catalyst
why: These are a compromise between rate, yield and cost.
